The solution heat treated alloy shows a signi ﬁcantly lower yield strength (about 350 MPa) compared to the aged alloy with yield strength close to 1200 MPa.
The solution heat treated alloy shows a signi ﬁcantly lower yield strength (about 350 MPa) compared to the aged alloy with yield strength close to 1200 MPa.

The strain hardening rate in the solution heat treated specimen, however, initially decrease rapidly to about 0.05 strain, then saturates temporarily at 2750 MPa, before decreasing steadily to 1750 MPa/unit strain.
From the curves, it can be noted that the strain hardening rate of the aged alloy decreases rapidly until it saturates to 1750 MPa/unit strain at 0.3 strain.
It can be observed that thermal softening is more pronounced in the aged specimen where strain hardening curve rapidly drops below zero at about 0.155 strain.
The solution heat treated specimen however, shows signi ﬁcant work hardening response to suppress the strain localisation, caused by thermal softening, until about 0.4 strain.
A signi ﬁcantly higher strain rate sensitivity can be noted in the solution heat treated samples in all the strain rate tested compared to the age-hardened specimen.

Under both loading conditions, the age-hardened alloys exhibit a greater ﬂow stress, compared to the solution heat treated alloy, which can be attributed to the stronger in ﬂuence of strengthening precipitates, in the age-hardened alloys, to impede the movement of dislocation.

In the peak aged condition, the strengthening of ATI 718Plus ® is believed to be provided by the anti-phase boundary (APB) effects from dislocation shearing of γ′ precipitates and coherency strain effects arising from the γ′–γ misﬁt.

Since the alloy deforms by the shearing of γ′ precipitates, it is proposed that, it is much easier for slip to occur within existing active planes of the aged alloy, where precipitates had already been sheared, than on other inactive slip systems [ 8 ].
This decreases the strain hardening behaviour of the age-hardened alloy, and tends to promote strain localisation as seen in the micrograph on Fig. 7b.

In contrast to the behaviour of the alloys under quasi-static loading, the effect of thermal softening is observed to quickly dominate the strain hardening response of the alloy under dynamic loading.
The inception of adiabatic heating leading to strain localisation occurs when the strain hardening rate curve of the material decreases below zero.

In the solution heat treated alloys, where the precipitates are very ﬁne and easily shearable, slip on hitherto inactive planes can be activated as the slip on the existing system becomes more dif ﬁcult, which can attest to the bulk deformation seen in the micrograph of the solution heat treated specimen in Fig. 7a.

Moreover, during dynamic loading of materials, it is known that signiﬁcant rate of strain hardening can aid the suppression of strain localisation that leads to the formation of detrimental adiabatic shear band. [ 13 ].
